summary: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of an integer array.
mainInsight: For each subsequence length keep only the smallest possible last element; that list stays sorted, so every new element is placed with a binary search and the list length is the answer.
invariant: tails is strictly increasing and tails[k] is the minimum last value over all increasing subsequences of length k + 1.

promptVariants: Why is it enough to remember only the smallest tail for each subsequence length?
Explain the idea behind the tails array.
cards.answer: For a fixed length, a smaller last value is always at least as good: anything that can extend the subsequence with a larger tail can also extend the one with a smaller tail. So for each length k + 1 we keep only the minimum possible last element. That list is increasing, so each new element can be placed with a binary search.
keyPoints: Smaller tail dominates a larger one
Tails sorted so binary search applies
cards.explanation: Dominance argument: a smaller tail never loses an extension opportunity.

promptVariants: Which statement is true about tails after every iteration?
What invariant does the tails list maintain?
options: It is strictly increasing and tails[k] is the minimum tail of any length k + 1 subsequence
It is a valid increasing subsequence of nums of maximum length so far
It holds the values of the longest subsequence in their original order of appearance
It is non-decreasing and tails[k] is the last element of the longest subsequence
cards.answer: It is strictly increasing and tails[k] is the minimum tail of any length k + 1 subsequence
cards.explanation: Only its length is guaranteed to equal the LIS so far; its entries are per-length minimum tails.

incorrectOptionExplanations.It is a valid increasing subsequence of: Not necessarily a subsequence of nums: for [2, 5, 3, 7, 1] it ends as [1, 3, 7] but 1 comes after 7.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It holds the values of the longest subse: Replacements break the original order, so it cannot be read as the actual subsequence.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It is non-decreasing and tails[k] is the: It is strictly increasing, and tails[k] belongs to length k + 1, not to the longest subsequence.

promptVariants: Why does the code use bisect_left rather than bisect_right?
What would bisect_right change about the answer?
options: Equal values must replace a tail because the increase has to be strict
Equal values must be appended so that duplicates extend the subsequence
bisect_left is the only variant that works on lists with duplicates
bisect_right would skip over the smallest element of tails
cards.answer: Equal values must replace a tail because the increase has to be strict
cards.explanation: bisect_left returns the first tail >= x, so an equal x overwrites that tail instead of extending. bisect_right would place equals after, and the list length would count non-decreasing subsequences.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Equal values must be appended so that du: That is the non-strict (non-decreasing) variant; this problem says strictly increasing.
incorrectOptionExplanations.bisect_left is the only variant that wor: Both work on duplicates; they differ in which side of equal elements they return.
incorrectOptionExplanations.bisect_right would skip over the smalles: It does not skip anything; it only lands after equal values.

cards.explanation: Processing 3 replaces 5, and 1 replaces 2, giving [1, 3, 7]. The value 1 comes after 7 in nums, so tails is only a bookkeeping array; its length equals the LIS length.

promptVariants: What does the canonical code return for nums = [2, 2, 3, 3], and why?

cards.answer: 2, because equal values replace tails instead of extending
cards.explanation: tails evolves [2] -> [2] -> [2, 3] -> [2, 3], so the strict LIS is 2; a non-decreasing LIS would be 4.

incorrectOptionExplanations.4, because equal values are allowed to e: That is the non-decreasing variant, not this problem.
incorrectOptionExplanations.3, because duplicates are only counted o: The strict LIS of the distinct values 2 and 3 is 2, not 3.
incorrectOptionExplanations.1, because the repeated 2 resets the lis: A repeated value overwrites an equal tail but never shrinks the list.

promptVariants: In your O(n^2) dp, which loop would a binary search replace, and what must be true for it to work?
How do you turn your dp into O(n log n)?
cards.answer: The inner `for j in range(i)` scan for the best earlier smaller element. It can be replaced by maintaining tails (the smallest tail per length), which is sorted, so a binary search finds the length that x can extend. The dp is quadratic in time with O(n) space; tails is n log n with O(n) space.
keyPoints: Inner loop scans all earlier elements
Binary search for the insertion position
cards.explanation: The dp answers 'best ending at i'; the tails array answers 'best tail for length k', which is monotone and therefore searchable.
